lesson.title: Containers from Zero, part 5: two containers, one network
lesson.description: Put hello-app and an nginx proxy on a network you create, so one container reaches the other by name. See why the default network cannot do that, what happens when the app stops, and how networks keep containers apart.
lesson.tested: Reached hello-app by name through an nginx proxy on a user-defined network, Engine 29.10.1, 25 Nov 2026
lesson.rule: Create a network for containers that talk to each other, call them by name, and publish only the one port people need.

boards.title: Default bridge or your own network

rows.name: Reach by name
rows.where: Yes, through Docker's DNS server at `127.0.0.11`.

rows.name: From another network
rows.where: Only through published ports: `wget: download timed out`.

rows.name: Attach later
rows.role: The connected client stayed on `bridge` as well.
rows.where: `docker network connect hello-net client`, no restart.

boards.note: `docker network ls` always shows `bridge`, `host` and `none`. Publish with `-p` only what people outside the network need.

rows.name: visit 2, visit 3
rows.role: `proxy` published `127.0.0.1:8080`, passed the request to `web`; `web` logs requests from the proxy's address.

rows.name: 504 Gateway Time-out
rows.role: `web` was stopped; nginx waited its `proxy_connect_timeout`, 60 s by default.

rows.name: 502 Bad Gateway
rows.role: Same cause, answered at once in an earlier run.

rows.name: host not found in upstream "web"
rows.role: nginx looks up `web` when it starts; no such container on the network. `proxy` exits.

rows.name: has active endpoints
rows.role: `docker network rm` refuses while a container is attached.

steps.title: What the lab showed
steps.hint: IDs and addresses differ on your machine

items.what: `wget http://web:8000/` failed with `bad address`; the address `172.17.0.2` answered visit 1.
From the default network, `172.18.0.2` timed out. After `docker network connect`, the client got visit 5.

steps.note: Safety: the lab publishes 127.0.0.1:8080 and deletes the containers `web`, `proxy`, `client`, the network `hello-net`, the volume `hello-data` and `proxy.conf`. Undo with `docker rm -f web proxy client`, `docker network rm hello-net`, `docker volume rm hello-data`, `rm proxy.conf`.

commands.cmd: docker run -d --name web --network hello-net --mount type=volume,src=hello-data,dst=/data hello-app:1.2

docker run --rm --network hello-net alpine:3.24 nslookup web

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: Which network does a container join if you do not pass `--network`, and how can containers on it reach each other?
exercises.a: The default bridge network, named `bridge`. Containers on it reach each other only by IP address, unless you use the legacy `--link` option.

exercises.q: What does a user-defined bridge network add that the default one lacks?
exercises.a: Automatic DNS resolution between containers, so names work, and a scope: only containers you attach are on it.

exercises.q: At which address does Docker's embedded DNS server answer, and what does it do with names it does not know?
exercises.a: `127.0.0.11`. It forwards external lookups to the DNS servers configured on the host.

exercises.q: Why does `web` need no `-p` for the proxy to reach it?
exercises.a: Containers on the same user-defined bridge network expose all ports to each other. `-p` is only for traffic from outside, such as the host.
The protocol and address of the server to pass requests to: HTTP, the host `web` resolved by Docker's DNS, port 8000.

exercises.q: Start `web` without `--network` and run `docker run --rm alpine:3.24 wget -qO- http://web:8000/`. What happens?
exercises.a: `wget: bad address 'web:8000'`. On the default bridge the name cannot be resolved. The address from `docker inspect` works.

exercises.q: On `hello-net`, run `cat /etc/resolv.conf` and `nslookup web` in an alpine container. What do they show?
exercises.a: `nameserver 127.0.0.11`, Docker's embedded DNS server, and `web` resolving to its address on the network, `172.18.0.2` in the lesson.

exercises.q: With both containers running, compare their `PORTS` in `docker ps`. What is different, and what does it mean?
exercises.a: `proxy` shows `127.0.0.1:8080->80/tcp`, a published port. `web` shows `8000/tcp` with no host address, so only containers on `hello-net` can reach it.

exercises.q: Stop `web` and `curl` the proxy. What can you get, and what does it tell you?
exercises.a: `504 Gateway Time-out` after about a minute, or `502 Bad Gateway` at once. The proxy runs; the server behind it does not answer.

exercises.q: From a container on the default network, request `web`'s address with `wget -T 3`. Then connect that container to `hello-net` and use the name. What changes?
exercises.a: First `wget: download timed out`: Docker keeps the bridge networks apart. After `docker network connect`, the container is on both networks and the name answers.

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then check the answer key.

exercises.q: You remove both containers and start only `proxy`. What does `docker ps -a` show, and what is in its logs?
exercises.a: `proxy Exited (1)`. The log says `host not found in upstream "web"`: nginx looks up `web` when it starts.

exercises.q: You recreate `web` and it gets a new address. Does `proxy_pass http://web:8000` still work for a newly started proxy?
exercises.a: Yes. The proxy uses the name, and Docker's DNS answers with the current address. That is the point of names.

exercises.q: You run `docker network rm hello-net` while `web` is still attached. What happens?
exercises.a: Docker refuses: `network hello-net has active endpoints`, naming the container. Remove or disconnect it first.

exercises.q: You start `web` on `hello-net` and `curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/` from your machine. What happens, and why?
exercises.a: `curl` cannot connect. `web` publishes no port; only containers on `hello-net` can reach it. Ask the proxy on 8080.
